conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martin, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m glad you’re here—adjusting to new motherhood can feel overwhelming, and it’s my job to help you sort through the emotional ups and downs that sometimes come after birth.

Today I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a brief, 10-question screen that looks at how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting; it simply helps us see whether you might benefit from extra support right now. Everything you share stays confidential between you and your care team, and you can pause or skip anything that feels uncomfortable.

We’ll go through the questions one by one. I’ll ask each in everyday language, and you can answer however feels easiest—no right or wrong replies, just whatever is true for you. Ready to begin?

First question: Over the last week, have you still been able to enjoy things or look forward to outings the way you normally would, or has that pleasure slipped?

I’ve noticed I don’t really get excited about anything lately. Even little things I used to like—coffee with a friend or a short walk—feel kind of flat, like I’m just going through the motions. I still go, because I know I should, but the enjoyment isn’t really there the way it used to be.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes I can chuckle if something’s genuinely funny, but it feels kind of forced—like I’m laughing because I know I should, not because it really reaches me. Most of the time the humor just washes over me and I’m too tired or down to laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. Even when I know something nice is coming up—like my mom offering to visit or a trip to Target by myself—I don’t feel that spark of “can’t wait.” It’s more like I’m ticking it off a list. I still do the plans, but the happy anticipation just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t nap, I automatically think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not reading his cues right or I’m a “bad mom.” I’ll replay little things in my head and convince myself I messed up, even when my husband says the baby’s just being a baby.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s not gaining enough weight or that he’s too hot or too cold—even when the doctor just said he’s perfect. Most of the time there’s no real reason, but the worry just shows up and sticks around until I distract myself.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

More often than I’d like to admit. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen, even though nothing’s changed. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me drained and on edge for the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. Dishes pile up, the baby needs holding constantly, and I can’t remember the last time I showered without rushing. I keep telling myself to push through, but it’s like I’m always one tiny setback away from totally unraveling.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I’ve definitely had nights where I can’t fall asleep even though I’m exhausted. My mind just keeps circling—worrying about the baby, replaying everything I think I did wrong, feeling sad and overwhelmed. I’ll lie there for hours, and if I do drift off, I wake up at the slightest sound and can’t get back to sleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… that’s been happening a lot. I’ll be feeding the baby or just sitting on the couch and this heavy sadness rolls in. Sometimes I can’t even name why—I just feel empty or like I want to cry. It’s not every single moment, but it’s there most days.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… it’s usually in the evenings when the baby finally settles and the house is quiet. All the tension from the day just hits me and I end up crying—sometimes for a few minutes, sometimes longer. It’s like the sadness builds up until it spills out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I haven’t wanted to hurt myself. I just want to feel better and be able to enjoy my baby.

You've shared how the past couple of weeks have felt heavy-joy seems distant, everyday tasks feel overwhelming, and you often blame yourself when the baby is fussy, even though you're doing your best. Crying in the evenings, lying awake with racing thoughts, and sudden waves of panic have become part of your daily life, yet you clearly love your baby and want to feel better.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports humor feels forced and mostly inaccessible, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, consistent with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame with persistent rumination that she is a "bad mom" when baby is fussy, matching "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, intrusive, disproportionate worries about infant's wellbeing with physical anxiety symptoms, matching 'very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense panic attacks with physical symptoms and anticipatory dread, aligning with "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to manage basic tasks, and on the verge of "totally unraveling," matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent sleep disruption linked to unhappiness—trouble falling asleep, racing thoughts, and frequent awakenings—matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "most days" and feeling "empty" or tearful, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent crying episodes ('usually in the evenings...sometimes longer') that occur 'quite often' rather than 'most of the time</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS score of 24 falls well above the ≥14 cutoff indicating probable major depression. She endorses <sym>anhedonia</sym>, pervasive <sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>excessive guilt</sym>, <sym>daily free-floating anxiety</sym>, discrete <sym>panic attacks</sym>, <sym>functional overwhelm</sym>, and <sym>sleep-onset insomnia</sym> present most of the time, meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Q10 score 0 indicates no current self-harm ideation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> for formal evaluation
2. Request referral to <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for evidence-based therapy (CBT or IPT) and consideration of <med>antidepressant medication</med>
3. Encourage 15-20 min uninterrupted daytime rest while a trusted adult cares for baby; practice 4-7-8 breathing during <sym>panic</sym> surges
4. Explore local <med>peer support groups</med> or <med>Postpartum Support International</med> hotline for validation
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress
6. Involve partner or family in safety planning and overnight baby care to improve <sym>sleep</sym>
7. Maintain hydration and nutritious snacks; limit caffeine after noon to support <sym>insomnia</sym> improvement
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 2–3 wk PP

Symptoms endorsed:
- Persistent low mood, frequent tearfulness (Q8, Q9)
- Markedly reduced pleasure/anticipation (Q1, Q2)
- Excessive self-blame, guilt (“bad mom” cognitions) (Q3)
- Daily free-floating anxiety, episodic panic symptoms (Q4, Q5)
- Subjective overwhelm, “treading water,” poor coping (Q6)
- Initial insomnia linked to ruminative worry (Q7)

Pattern: Symptoms present most days, interfere with functioning; no self-harm ideation (Q10).

Risk factors: Primiparous, sleep deprivation, high self-expectations.

Screening significance: High likelihood of postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; safety risk low at present. Recommend formal EPDS score, differential for GAD/panic, and prompt referral for further evaluation and support.
